objectives: Explain what LayerNorm normalizes and why

slides.title: Part 1 — Keeping a deep stack stable
slides.body: Stack 50 layers without normalization and activations drift by orders of magnitude; the loss plateaus and nothing trains. Layer normalization is one of the two tricks (the other is residuals) that make deep transformers possible at all.

slides.title: What layer norm does
slides.body:
For each token's vector, **per token, across the feature dimension**:

1. Compute mean $\mu$ and std $\sigma$ over the $d_{model}$ features.
2. Normalize: subtract $\mu$, divide by $\sigma$.
3. Apply learned scale $\gamma$ and shift $\beta$:

$$\text{LN}(x)=\gamma\cdot\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma+\epsilon}+\beta$$

The activation panel on the right shows what unnormalized vs normalized activations look like across a layer — the normalized ones stay on a stable scale instead of drifting. The defining property: LN is computed **per token**, independent of batch and sequence length.

slides.title: Layer norm vs batch norm
slides.body:
Both normalize, over **different axes**:

- **Batch norm:** per *feature*, across the *batch*.
- **Layer norm:** per *example/token*, across its *features*.

Why it matters for transformers:

- **Inference parity.** Batch norm uses per-batch stats at train time and running averages at inference — forget to switch and predictions silently corrupt. Layer norm is identical in both.
- **Variable length.** Transformers process variable-length, padded sequences; batch norm's batch stats get confused, layer norm doesn't care.

question.question: For an input of shape [batch, seq_len, d_model], which axis does layer norm reduce over?
question.explanation: For each (batch, seq position), LN computes mean/std across the d_model feature axis. That batch- and length-independence is exactly why it behaves identically at training and inference — the whole reason it replaced batch norm in transformers.

question.question: A model trained with batch norm is served at batch_size = 1 in training mode. What breaks?
options: Per-batch stats become meaningless (the 'mean' is the single input); only running-average eval mode is correct — forgetting to switch silently corrupts outputs
Nothing — batch norm is batch-size independent
Activations always explode regardless of mode
question.explanation: Batch norm has two stat sources: per-batch (train) and running averages (eval). At batch_size = 1 the per-batch 'statistics' are degenerate. `model.eval()` switches to running averages; forgetting it is a classic deployment bug. Layer norm sidesteps it entirely.

slides.title: Part 2 — Placement and the modern variant
Pre-norm vs post-norm
slides.body:
Where LN sits relative to the residual add matters at depth:

**Post-norm** (original): `out = LN(x + Sublayer(x))`

**Pre-norm** (GPT-2 onward): `out = x + Sublayer(LN(x))`

In pre-norm the residual stream itself is never normalized — the clean identity path is preserved, so very deep stacks train stably. Post-norm normalizes the stream every layer, which destabilizes deep models. Every modern large model uses **pre-norm**; post-norm is mostly historical (it can edge out the final loss when it *does* train, but pre-norm is the safe default).

slides.title: RMSNorm
slides.body:
**RMSNorm** drops the mean-subtraction, normalizing only the magnitude:

$$\text{RMSNorm}(x)=\gamma\cdot\frac{x}{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{d}\sum_i x_i^2}}$$

Empirically the mean-centering term contributes little for transformers, so RMSNorm matches or beats LayerNorm at slightly less compute. LLaMA, Mistral, and most modern open models use it. If a model card says `RMSNorm`, read it as "LayerNorm minus the recentering."

question.question: Why did large models migrate from post-norm to pre-norm?
options: Pre-norm leaves the residual stream un-normalized, preserving the identity path so very deep stacks train stably
Post-norm cannot represent the same functions
Pre-norm removes the need for residual connections
question.explanation: Pre-norm normalizes only the *input* to each sublayer; the residual stream flows through unnormalized, keeping a clean gradient highway across depth. Post-norm renormalizes the stream every layer, which causes instability as depth grows — fatal for 50–100 layer models.

slides.title: What to carry forward
slides.body:
- LN normalizes **per token across features** → batch/length independent, identical at train & inference.
- Not batch norm — different axis, no eval-mode footgun.
- **Pre-norm** placement is the modern default for trainable depth; **RMSNorm** is the common simplification.

**Next:** [Residual connections](/wiki/residual-connections) — the other half of "why deep transformers train" — then the full [transformer block](/wiki/transformer-block).
